It does not generally prove that \[ p\mapsto \log\|X\|_p = \frac1p\log E|X|^p \] is convex. Indeed, for \(p_1,p_2\in[1,p_0)\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), define \[ p=\lambda p_1+(1-\lambda)p_2. \] Then \[ |X|^p = |X|^{\lambda p_1+(1-\lambda)p_2} = |X|^{\lambda p_1}|X|^{(1-\lambda)p_2}. \] Use Hölder’s inequality with conjugate exponents \[ r=\frac1\lambda, \qquad s=\frac1{1-\lambda}. \] Then \[ \frac1r+\frac1s = \lambda+(1-\lambda) = 1. \] So \[ E|X|^p = E\left(|X|^{\lambda p_1}|X|^{(1-\lambda)p_2}\right) \le \left(E|X|^{p_1}\right)^\lambda \left(E|X|^{p_2}\right)^{1-\lambda}. \] Taking logarithms gives \[ \log E|X|^p \le \lambda\log E|X|^{p_1} + (1-\lambda)\log E|X|^{p_2}. \] Therefore, \[ p\mapsto \log E|X|^p \] is convex on \([1,p_0)\). Equivalently, \[ E|X|^p \] is log-convex in \(p\). In terms of \(L_p\)-norms, this gives \[ \|X\|_p^p \le \left(\|X\|_{p_1}^{p_1}\right)^\lambda \left(\|X\|_{p_2}^{p_2}\right)^{1-\lambda}. \] That is, \[ \|X\|_p \le \|X\|_{p_1}^{\lambda p_1/p} \|X\|_{p_2}^{(1-\lambda)p_2/p}. \] This is the interpolation inequality obtained from Hölder’s inequality. Ex 28 Suppose \(u\) is a continuous and increasing mapping of \([0,\infty]\) onto \([0,\infty]\). Let \(u^{-1}\) be its inverse function. Define, for \(x\ge0\), \[ U(x)=\int_0^x u(s)\,ds, \qquad V(x)=\int_0^x u^{-1}(s)\,ds. \] Show \[ xy\le U(x)+V(y), \qquad x,y\in[0,\infty]. \] Hence, for two random variables \(X,Y\) on the same probability space, \(XY\) is integrable if \[ U(|X|)\in L_1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad V(|Y|)\in L_1. \] Specialize to the case where \[ u(x)=x^{p-1}, \qquad p>1. \] \(\textbf{Answer:}\) First consider \[ x,y\in(0,\infty). \] Fix \[ x_0\in(0,\infty), \] and let \[ y_0=u(x_0). \] Since \(u\) is increasing and continuous, \(u^{-1}\) is also increasing. Also, \[ U(x)=\int_0^x u(s)\,ds, \qquad V(y)=\int_0^y u^{-1}(s)\,ds. \] We prove \[ x_0y\le U(x_0)+V(y) \] by considering three cases. Case 1: \(y=y_0\) Since \[ y_0=u(x_0), \] the rectangle with side lengths \(x_0\) and \(y_0\) is divided by the curve \(y=u(x)\) into two regions. Hence \[ x_0y_0=U(x_0)+V(y_0). \] Therefore, \[ x_0y=U(x_0)+V(y). \] Case 2: \(y<y_0\) Let \[ a=u^{-1}(y). \] Then \[ a<x_0. \] Since \(y=u(a)\), we have \[ ay=U(a)+V(y). \] Therefore, \[ x_0y = ay+(x_0-a)y = U(a)+V(y)+(x_0-a)y. \] Since \(u\) is increasing, for \(s\in[a,x_0]\), \[ u(s)\ge u(a)=y. \] Thus \[ (x_0-a)y \le \int_a^{x_0}u(s)\,ds. \] Hence \[ x_0y \le U(a)+V(y)+\int_a^{x_0}u(s)\,ds. \] Since \[ U(x_0)=U(a)+\int_a^{x_0}u(s)\,ds, \] we get \[ x_0y\le U(x_0)+V(y). \] Case 3: \(y>y_0\) Since \[ x_0y_0=U(x_0)+V(y_0), \] we have \[ x_0y = x_0y_0+x_0(y-y_0) = U(x_0)+V(y_0)+x_0(y-y_0). \] For \(s\in[y_0,y]\), since \(u^{-1}\) is increasing, \[ u^{-1}(s)\ge u^{-1}(y_0)=x_0. \] Therefore, \[ x_0(y-y_0) \le \int_{y_0}^{y}u^{-1}(s)\,ds. \] Hence \[ x_0y \le U(x_0)+V(y_0)+\int_{y_0}^{y}u^{-1}(s)\,ds. \] Since \[ V(y)=V(y_0)+\int_{y_0}^{y}u^{-1}(s)\,ds, \] we get \[ x_0y\le U(x_0)+V(y). \] Combining the three cases, for all \[ x,y\in(0,\infty), \] we have \[ xy\le U(x)+V(y). \] The cases \(x=0\) or \(y=0\) are immediate. The endpoint or infinite cases follow by monotone limiting from the finite positive case. Therefore, \[ xy\le U(x)+V(y), \qquad x,y\in[0,\infty]. \] Now let \(X,Y\) be random variables on the same probability space. Applying the inequality with \[ x=|X|, \qquad y=|Y|, \] we get \[ |XY| = |X||Y| \le U(|X|)+V(|Y|). \] If \[ U(|X|)\in L_1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad V(|Y|)\in L_1, \] then \[ E[U(|X|)]<\infty \qquad\text{and}\qquad E[V(|Y|)]<\infty. \] Therefore, \[ E|XY| \le E[U(|X|)]+E[V(|Y|)] <\infty. \] Thus \[ XY\in L_1. \] Now specialize to \[ u(x)=x^{p-1}, \qquad p>1. \] Then \[ u^{-1}(y)=y^{1/(p-1)}. \] So \[ U(x) = \int_0^x s^{p-1}\,ds = \frac{x^p}{p}. \] Also, \[ V(y) = \int_0^y s^{1/(p-1)}\,ds. \] Since \[ \frac{1}{p-1}+1 = \frac{p}{p-1}, \] we get \[ V(y) = \frac{p-1}{p}y^{p/(p-1)}. \] Let \[ q=\frac{p}{p-1}. \] Then \[ \frac1p+\frac1q = \frac1p+\frac{p-1}{p} = 1. \] Also, \[ \frac{p-1}{p} = \frac1q. \] Thus \[ V(y)=\frac{y^q}{q}. \] Young’s inequality becomes \[ xy \le \frac{x^p}{p} + \frac{y^q}{q}. \] Applying this to \[ x=|X|, \qquad y=|Y|, \] we obtain \[ |XY| \le \frac{|X|^p}{p} + \frac{|Y|^q}{q}. \] Taking expectations gives \[ E|XY| \le \frac1pE|X|^p + \frac1qE|Y|^q. \] Therefore, if \[ X\in L_p \qquad\text{and}\qquad Y\in L_q, \] where \[ \frac1p+\frac1q=1, \] then \[ XY\in L_1. \] \(\textbf{Note:}\) What we have done in this exercise is called the Young’s Inequality, and we can deduce Holder’s Inequality from it.
